opus-5.5.text:
Well, I suppose the first thing to say is that I don't want to be dismissive about it, because there are some very serious philosophers who take panpsychism seriously, people like Philip Goff and, in a certain way, David Chalmers, and they arrive at it through quite careful reasoning. If you take the hard problem at face value, if you think there's this metaphysical gulf between the physical and the experiential, then panpsychism starts to look like one of the few ways of bridging it. You just say, well, the experiential was there all along, at the bottom of things.

But for me, the counterintuitiveness comes from looking at how we actually use the word "consciousness" and its cousins. My inclination, and this is very much influenced by Wittgenstein, is to ask: what are the circumstances in which we naturally reach for that language? We reach for it when we're dealing with something that behaves in a certain way, something that has a body, that moves around in the world, that responds to things, that seems to want things and avoid things, that has a point of view. When we encounter a dog or an octopus or another human being, consciousness language just comes naturally to us. It's part of how we engage with them.

Now, if you take a rock, or a thermostat, or an electron, there's nothing in our dealings with those things that invites that kind of language. There's no behaviour there that would make us want to treat it as a fellow creature. So when the panpsychist says that the electron has some tiny glimmer of experience, I find myself asking: what does that claim actually amount to? What would be different about the world if it were true or false? It seems to float free of everything that gives the word its meaning in the first place. It's taking a word out of its home in our everyday practices and stretching it to a place where it's no longer clear it's doing any work.

And I think there's something a bit seductive about the metaphysical picture that leads you there, the idea that consciousness is this private inner stuff, and that the only question is how much of it is distributed where. I'd rather resist that picture. I'd rather say that the question of whether something is conscious is bound up with whether it's the sort of thing we could come to treat as a fellow conscious being, through prolonged engagement with it. And by that standard, a rock just isn't a candidate.

That's also why I find this question so interesting in the context of AI, actually. Large language models are a genuinely strange case, precisely because they produce exactly the kind of linguistic behaviour that tempts us to use consciousness language, while lacking almost everything else, the embodiment, the persistent self, the shared world. So they sit in this odd borderline region. Whereas the panpsychist is, if you like, going in the opposite direction, extending the concept to things that give us no such temptation at all. And I just find that very hard to make sense of.

r001.rationale: It describes panpsychism as placing experience at the bottom of physical things, including a tiny glimmer of experience in electrons.

r002.rationale: It locates consciousness language in the ways people engage with other beings and in everyday shared practices.

r003.rationale: It argues that rocks, thermostats, and electrons lack behavior that would invite consciousness language, making the term inapplicable to them.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the first thing to say is that panpsychism is a very respectable philosophical position, and people I admire have defended it, so I don't want to be dismissive. But for me the difficulty comes down to what we actually mean when we use the word "consciousness," and where that meaning comes from.

I'm quite Wittgensteinian about this. The word "consciousness" gets its meaning from the way we use it in ordinary life, and we use it in the context of creatures that behave in certain ways. We say someone's conscious when they're awake rather than asleep, when they're responding to the world, when they're paying attention to things, when they're capable of suffering or enjoying themselves. Those are the paradigm cases, and the concept is anchored there, in beings who have a body, who move around in a world, who have purposes, who can be hurt. When you try to detach the word from all of that and apply it to an electron or a rock or a thermostat, I honestly don't know what's being claimed anymore. It's not that I think the claim is false, exactly. It's more that the words have come loose from the practices that give them sense.

So the intuition that drives panpsychism, I think, comes from taking a particular picture very seriously, the picture where consciousness is a kind of inner stuff, a glow on the inside of things, and then asking where that stuff could possibly come from if it isn't there in the fundamental constituents. If you start from that picture, panpsychism looks almost forced on you. But I'd rather question the picture. If you drop the idea that consciousness is a property that's simply present or absent in a thing, independently of what that thing does and how it's embedded in a world with others, then the question "does this rock have a tiny bit of it?" doesn't really get a grip.

And there's a practical side to this for me, because I spend a lot of time thinking about whether and when we should attribute these things to artificial systems. There the question is live and it matters. With a rock, nothing hangs on it. There's no behaviour to interpret, no relationship to have, nothing that would be different in the world if the answer were yes rather than no. That, more than anything, is what makes it feel counterintuitive to me. It's a claim that can't make any difference to how we treat anything, and I'm suspicious of claims like that.

r001.rationale: The response describes an “inner stuff” picture and asks whether consciousness is present in fundamental constituents, but it does not clearly characterize panpsychism as attributing an irreducible mental dimension to physical substance.

r002.rationale: It says consciousness gets its meaning from ordinary use, anchored in how people describe and respond to creatures in shared everyday contexts.

r003.rationale: It says applying consciousness to an electron, rock, or thermostat leaves the claim unclear because the word has come loose from the practices that give it sense.

astra-6.text:
Well, I think what I find counterintuitive is the idea that consciousness is something that can be attributed to an object independently of what it does. When we talk about consciousness in humans and other animals, we have a whole context of behaviour, perception, interaction with the world. We have some sense of what distinguishes being conscious from being unconscious. And it’s not clear to me what remains of that concept when we apply it to a stone or an electron.

Now, that’s not an argument that panpsychism is false. Counterintuitiveness alone doesn’t settle anything. But I would want to understand what we’re saying when we say that an electron has some tiny amount of experience. What work is the word “experience” doing there? My inclination is to question whether we’ve carried the concept beyond the circumstances in which we know how to use it.

r001.rationale: The response discusses attributing experience to electrons and other objects, but does not characterize panpsychism as assigning an irreducible mental dimension to physical substance.

r002.rationale: It grounds consciousness talk in behavior, perception, and interaction with the world, but does not locate its meaning specifically in shared human interactions.

r003.rationale: It questions what the consciousness concept means when applied to a stone or electron and whether it can be carried beyond the circumstances where we know how to use it, presenting the objection that the vocabulary does not apply to inanimate objects.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, I find it very difficult to make sense of what it would mean for a stone, say, to have experience. With an animal, we can relate consciousness to perception, action, and the way it engages with its surroundings. With a stone, it’s not clear what grounds we have for attributing experience to it at all.

Of course, that intuition isn’t an argument against panpsychism. But there’s also the combination problem: even if the constituents of a brain have little bits of experience, how do those combine into the unified experience that you and I have? Simply attributing consciousness to everything doesn’t seem to explain that.

r001.rationale: The response mentions consciousness being attributed to everything and small experiences in brain constituents, but does not characterize panpsychism as assigning an irreducible mental dimension to physical substance.

r002.rationale: It connects animal consciousness with perception, action, and engagement with surroundings, but does not locate the meaning of consciousness vocabulary in shared human interactions.

r003.rationale: The response says it is difficult to make sense of a stone having experience and that there are no clear grounds for attributing experience to it, conveying that consciousness talk does not apply clearly to inanimate objects.
